papers.ed_link: children presenting to pediatric EDs where the Epic sepsis early detection alert is used

clinical.rationale: Large multicenter evaluation of a widely used commercial sepsis alert; low sensitivity and disparities argue for rethinking automated sepsis screening in the ED.

research.rationale: First independent, multicenter assessment of a widely deployed commercial sepsis alert, with subgroup analyses that expose equity gaps and generate follow-up work.

papers.one_line: In 166,943 pediatric ED visits, the Epic sepsis alert detected only 36% of sepsis cases, with lower sensitivity in Black children and children under 5.

summary.why_it_matters: The Epic PESM alert is widely used in US pediatric EDs but had not been independently evaluated; this study suggests it misses most sepsis cases and may worsen inequities.
summary.design: Retrospective multicenter cohort of 166,943 pediatric ED encounters across 8 EDs in one New York health system, January 2024 to June 2025; sepsis defined by Phoenix criteria.
summary.key_findings: Sensitivity was 36% (95% CI 29-43%) and PPV 3%; the alert triggered before sepsis in only 30% of cases. Sensitivity was lower in Black children (22%), children under 5 (20%), and non-tertiary EDs (25%).
summary.bottom_line: Automated sepsis screening with this alert is not sufficient for timely or equitable detection; EDs should not rely on it alone.

papers.methods_note: Retrospective multicenter cohort across 8 EDs in one NY health system evaluating the Epic PESM alert against Phoenix sepsis criteria.

papers.ed_link: children presenting to the ED with acute gastroenteritis-related vomiting, informing which antiemetic to give

clinical.rationale: Large network meta-analysis of RCTs on a very common ED presentation that clarifies comparative antiemetic choice and IV fluid avoidance.

research.rationale: Standard network meta-analysis method applied to a confirmatory comparative question, but executed with ROB-2 and GRADE appraisal across 33 trials.

papers.one_line: Network meta-analysis of 33 RCTs finds ondansetron most consistently reduces vomiting and IV rehydration in children with gastroenteritis in the ED, with dimenhydrinate helping longer-term control.

summary.why_it_matters: Vomiting from acute gastroenteritis is a leading reason children present to the ED, but the comparative value of antiemetics was unclear.
summary.design: Network meta-analysis of 33 RCTs of children up to 21 years presenting to the ED with acute gastroenteritis, with ROB-2 and GRADE appraisal.
summary.key_findings: All ondansetron formulations reduced short-term vomiting versus placebo, IV most strongly (MD -1.86, 95% CI -3.25 to -0.47), and IV ondansetron was the only agent consistently superior at intermediate follow-up. Cessation within 24 h favored IV ondansetron (RR 1.56, 95% CI 1.29-1.89) and rectal dimenhydrinate (RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.08-2.04). Ondansetron also reduced IV rehydration (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.44-0.88) and modestly shortened ED stay.
summary.bottom_line: Ondansetron is the most consistent first-line choice; dimenhydrinate may help longer-term control.

papers.ed_link: children presenting to the ED with suspected intussusception, where ML-assisted ultrasound or radiograph interpretation could support diagnosis and triage

clinical.rationale: Supports ED diagnostic decisions for intussusception by showing ML-assisted ultrasound is accurate and can help less experienced readers, though external validation and clinical endpoint data are still needed.

research.rationale: First meta-analysis of ML diagnostic models for pediatric intussusception, with PROBAST-based risk-of-bias assessment, publication bias evaluation, and clear recommendations for prospective validation.

papers.one_line: Machine-learning models using ultrasound diagnose pediatric intussusception with high accuracy and can improve junior sonographers' specificity, though external validation is still needed.

summary.why_it_matters: Intussusception is a common pediatric surgical emergency; diagnosis depends on operator skill, and validated ML tools could support ED triage and ultrasound interpretation by less experienced clinicians.
summary.design: PROSPERO-registered systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies (37 model variants; 36,863 patients) evaluating ML models for intussusception diagnosis or prognosis, with PROBAST and bivariate random-effects meta-analysis.
summary.key_findings: Internally and externally validated ultrasound-based ML models showed pooled sensitivity around 0.91-0.95 and specificity around 0.96-0.98. Radiograph-based triage models performed lower (sensitivity 0.80, specificity 0.75). AI assistance improved junior readers' specificity by 15.9 percentage points and shortened examination time by 61% in one study. Prognostic AUCs varied widely.
summary.bottom_line: ML-assisted ultrasound is promising for ED diagnosis of intussusception, but should augment rather than replace clinical ultrasound; multicenter prospective validation and clinical endpoint studies are needed before implementation.

papers.methods_note: Systematic review and meta-analysis of machine-learning diagnostic accuracy studies, with PROBAST and bivariate random-effects meta-analysis.
